name: submit_training_recommendation
content:
{
  "headline": "Your strength is dropping across all lifts—take a deload week to recover before continuing.",
  "summary": "You logged good volume this week with 56 sets and reasonable distribution across muscle groups, but your strength index has declined noticeably across nearly every lift. Combined with your reported joint aches, fatigue, and deteriorating session quality, this is a clear signal of accumulated fatigue. A planned deload is the right move to let your body recover and preserve long-term progress toward your muscle-building goal.",
  "progressiveOverload": {
    "status": "regressing",
    "notes": "Strength index has declined across all major muscle groups: chest dropped from 105 to 99, back from 104 to 98, legs from 104 to 97, and shoulders from 103 to 99. Only biceps and triceps are relatively stable at 100 and 100 respectively, suggesting upper-body isolation work is holding up but pressing and pulling strength is clearly compromised. This pattern, paired with your notes of worsening sessions, indicates acute overtraining rather than a single weak lift."
  },
  "muscleImbalances": [],
  "deloadRecommended": true,
  "deloadReason": "Strength declining across all major lifts, joint pain, persistent fatigue, and deteriorating session performance all point to accumulated nervous-system and systemic fatigue. A deload week will allow recovery without losing fitness.",
  "actionItems": [
    "Take a full deload week next period: reduce volume by 40–50 percent, drop intensity to perceived RPE 6–7 out of 10, and focus on movement quality and recovery rather than numbers.",
    "Prioritize sleep, nutrition, and stress management over the next 7–10 days; aim for 7–9 hours of sleep and ensure adequate protein and calories to support muscle building.",
    "After the deload, return to your previous progression with a fresh perspective; if pain or fatigue persists, reduce frequency or volume by one session or one exercise per muscle group.",
    "Track how you feel during the deload—if your joints stay achy or fatigue doesn't lift, consider consulting a healthcare provider to rule out underlying issues."
  ],
  "contextSummary": "Strength regressed this week after previously steady progress; joint pain and fatigue became limiting factors, signaling overtraining and the need for recovery before resuming hypertrophy work."
}
